title: The struggle for Saudi Arabia’s buried past
gist: A written essay (despite the podcast URL) crediting Andrea Valentino argues Saudi Arabia's $20bn Al-Ula archaeology-tourism bet is politically fragile: the same dynasty destroyed over 98 per cent of the kingdom's historical and religious sites since 1985 per the Islamic Heritage Research Foundation, MBS's Neom has had minimal archaeological survey, and Mecca's Ottoman fortress was flattened partly to make room for a $15bn hotel complex.

insights.claim: Al-Ula, the vast ancient site encompassing the Nabatean tomb Qasr Al-Farid, is set to receive investments worth $20bn, alongside academic conferences, research centres, a scheme pushing young Saudis into archaeology and a documentary narrated by Jeremy Irons.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: A concrete, sized allocation within Saudi diversification spending — heritage tourism is now a capital-project category alongside Neom and sport.
insights.locator: His ambition is obvious financially

insights.claim: With oil no longer a sure bet the Saudi government is rushing to divest, and hopes archaeological sites will help bring 150 million tourists to the kingdom by 2030.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: A hard, dated target investors can mark to market — hotel, aviation and construction exposure to Saudi hinges on progress against it.
insights.quote: With oil no longer a sure bet, the government is rushing to divest.
insights.locator: This bubbling activity can be understood in two ways

insights.claim: MBS's interest in pre-Islamic ruins is political as well as economic: they are vivid symbols of a new Saudi Arabia that distinguish his rule from his Wahhabi forebears and help crush the power of conservative clerics.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Archaeology is being used as an instrument of domestic political consolidation, which means its funding is only as durable as that political need.
insights.locator: Keen to distinguish his rule from his Wahhabi forebears

insights.claim: MBS declared in 2021 that 'Our people will amaze the world again', and the then CEO of the Royal Commission for Al-Ula said in January 2022 that the more they learn about ancient northwestern Arabians the more their mission reflects that mindset — an official who has since been arrested for corruption.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Key personnel behind the flagship heritage programme are subject to arbitrary removal — execution risk in Saudi megaprojects is personnel risk.
insights.quote: That official has since been arrested for corruption
insights.locator: ‘Our people,’ proclaimed Mohammed bin Salman in 2021

themes.theme: A documented record of heritage destruction

insights.claim: According to the Islamic Heritage Research Foundation, over 98 per cent of Saudi Arabia's historical and religious sites have been destroyed since 1985.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: The single hardest number in the piece and the strongest argument that the current preservation turn is an anomaly, not a trend.
insights.quote: over 98 per cent of the nation’s historical and religious sites have been destroyed since 1985
insights.locator: According to the Islamic Heritage Research Foundation

insights.claim: In 1994 a council of Saudi clerics issued an edict arguing that preserving historical sites could lead to polytheism and idolatry — both capital offences in the kingdom — and fifteen years later a prominent imam said non-Muslim archaeological discoveries are best left underground.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Formal religious rulings, not informal neglect, drove the destruction — meaning a reversal of clerical authority is what the current policy depends on.
insights.locator: In 1994, a council of local clerics issued an edict

insights.claim: Around 150 important pre-Muslim sites have vanished in Saudi Arabia and Mecca's eighteenth-century Ottoman castle was flattened in 2002, showing the demolition programme targeted non-Wahhabist Islamic heritage as well as pagan remains.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Establishes destruction as systematic and ideologically broad rather than incidental to development.
insights.locator: And if the diggers have been happy targeting symbols

insights.claim: In the 1970s the area around Qasr Al-Farid was subject to an official fatwa warning Muslims not to visit, with nearby roads lined with billboards urging people to discover Islam instead — the same site now marketed as a tourism icon.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: The flagship asset was under an official visit ban within living memory — a precise measure of how fast and how far Saudi policy can swing.
insights.locator: In the 1970s, the area around Qasr Al-Farid

insights.claim: The Ottoman fortress in Mecca was demolished partly for ideological reasons but also because the land was needed for a $15bn hotel complex, meaning commercial land value has already overridden heritage once at the largest scale.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Where heritage and high-value development compete in Saudi Arabia, the historical precedent points one way — a real risk to any preservation-dependent investment.
insights.quote: Recall, for instance, that the Ottoman fortress in Mecca was demolished partly for ideological reasons – but also because the land was needed for a $15bn hotel complex.
insights.locator: Recall, for instance, that the Ottoman fortress

insights.claim: MBS's landmark Neom project already seems to be putting profit before patrimony, with experts at the Endangered Archaeology in the Middle East and North Africa group warning that archaeological surveys of the planned city have been minimal even though the area could conceal monuments spanning thousands of years.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Neom carries a specific, credentialed heritage-compliance criticism that could become a reputational or UNESCO-facing liability.
insights.quote: Remarkably, MBS’s landmark Neom project already seems to be putting profit before patrimony.
insights.locator: Remarkably, MBS’s landmark Neom project

insights.claim: Saudi warplanes razed several ancient sites during the long bombing campaign in Yemen supported by MBS, including a 2015 airstrike that left a yawning gap in the Mar'ib Dam, and some of this destruction looks deliberate — an 'erasure' of Yemen's cultural identity in one scholar's phrase.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: The same regime marketing heritage at home bombed it next door — a contradiction that undercuts the reputational value of the Al-Ula programme.
insights.locator: MBS hasn’t shown much regard for heritage elsewhere

insights.claim: UNESCO last year placed the Sabean ruins at Mar'ib on its List of World Heritage in Danger, and combined with jihadi iconoclasm the future of southern Arabia's history looks bleak.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Formal international designation of danger is the closest thing to a public rating on regional heritage risk.
insights.locator: No wonder UNESCO last year put the Sabean ruins

themes.theme: Political fragility of the archaeological turn

insights.claim: Regime change in Riyadh could threaten icons such as Qasr Al-Farid, because on the historical record MBS's fellow Sauds have proved consummate wreckers for literally centuries, and even MBS himself may yet be tempted to call out the bulldozers.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Political-continuity risk is the central variable for any long-dated Saudi tourism or cultural-infrastructure exposure.
insights.quote: If, after all, we take history as a guide, his fellow Sauds have proved consummate wreckers for literally centuries.
insights.locator: MBS’s political dominance aside, in short

insights.claim: Conservative Saudis are deeply uneasy about how MBS has hawked the nation's past: last year a prominent cleric fled abroad after accusing him of 'replacing' the country's Muslim identity, and Saudis online have written that jahiliyya has returned to the Arabian Peninsula.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Suppressed conservative opposition is a latent constituency that a future leadership could mobilise against the heritage and liberalisation agenda.
insights.quote: ‘What’s happening at Al-Ula is very dangerous,’ wrote one in 2022. ‘I believe that jahiliyya has returned to the Arabian Peninsula.’
insights.locator: But there are signs that conservative Saudis

insights.claim: The jahiliyya concept — the 'age of ignorance' framing of pre-Islamic Arabia — has a long polemical afterlife, invoked by the thirteenth-century theologian Ibn Taymiyya against the Mongol khans and remaining popular with modern Islamists such as Sayyid Qutb.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: The ideological vocabulary for reversing the heritage policy is fully formed and eight centuries old — the reversal requires no new argument.
insights.locator: These ideas, which characterised the Arabs as rampaging pagans

insights.claim: Neighbouring Qatar and Bahrain have welcomed curious archaeologists for decades, showing that Gulf heritage policy is a state choice rather than a regional religious constraint.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Cross-Gulf comparison isolates Saudi-specific policy risk from generic regional risk.
insights.locator: To be fair, neighbouring countries took a more relaxed approach

insights.claim: Researchers at Al-Ula alone are finding tens of thousands of artefacts a year, from mother-of-pearl pendants to grand statues of broad-shouldered kings, plus Nabatean graves aligned to the rising and setting of the sun and moon.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: The discovery rate justifies the investment case on content grounds — the pipeline of new attractions is real, not promotional.
insights.locator: At Al-Ula alone, researchers are finding

insights.claim: Philologist Ahmad Al-Jallad has argued from new inscriptions around Mecca and Medina that some Arabian pagans were cautiously adopting obscure forms of monotheism, referencing 'Alh' and 'Lh', before they ever embraced the Allah of Islam.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Findings that complicate the founding narrative of Islam are the specific reason this research programme carries political risk.
insights.locator: Relying on a new batch of inscriptions

insights.claim: In the United Arab Emirates archaeologists hunting for a mosque or fort instead found an ancient monastery occupied until the mid-eighth century, complete with church and refectory, suggesting Christianity and Islam coexisted long after Muhammad's revelation and that the site may have rivalled established centres of Christian learning.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Hard physical evidence dismantling the clean-break narrative of Islam's arrival — the kind of finding that draws official discomfort.
insights.locator: In the United Arab Emirates, a team of archaeologists

insights.claim: Recently unearthed inscriptions near Al-Mandaq, about 230 miles south of Jeddah, show Arabic calligraphy was partly shaped by Middle Persian with a Nabatean flavour too.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Even the script itself turns out to be a cross-cultural product, further eroding the isolationist origin story.
insights.locator: At a remote site near Al-Mandaq

insights.claim: Historians have long been forced to lean on literary sources hostile to pre-Islamic Arabia — outsiders who characterised Arabians as mindless barbarians who 'practise no craft, trade, or agriculture at all' — because the only indigenous writing consists of short scratched inscriptions.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: A source-availability bias, not evidence, produced the consensus view — the general lesson that absence of records gets read as absence of sophistication.
insights.quote: ‘They practise no craft, trade, or agriculture at all,’ said one monastic account of the fifth century or sixth century, ‘but use the dagger alone as their means of subsistence.’
insights.locator: How can these difficulties be explained?

insights.claim: Ancient Arabia was commercially and religiously cosmopolitan rather than isolated: Nabateans carried the most valuable kinds of spices to the Mediterranean using waterproof cement that survives today, Sabeans grew rich on frankincense and myrrh and built the roughly 550-metre Mar'ib Dam irrigating thousands of acres, and Gulf inhabitants sold incense to Greece and traded to India.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: The historical baseline for Gulf trade cosmopolitanism is two millennia deep — a narrative asset states are now actively monetising.
insights.locator: It’s tempting to think of ancient Arabia

insights.claim: The Saudi National Antiquities Register recently announced it was adding 70 sites to its roster, a practical signal of institutionalisation alongside the research boom.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Formal registration is the mechanism that would make future demolition legally and reputationally costlier — worth tracking as a commitment indicator.
insights.locator: Together with more practical developments
